newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin under fire on family allowances.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin under fire on family allowances.

text.p: New Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin faced the first test of his resolve on Tuesday when protesters demonstrated against his plan to withdraw generous family allowances from the better-off and his Communist coalition partners voiced opposition.

More than 500 well-heeled activists, including many mothers with young children, demonstrated outside parliament, supported by members of the conservative opposition, with banners proclaiming "Don't swipe my allowance".
Some of the women pushed prams or carried toddlers in their arms as they waved placards denouncing the Socialist premier or comparing him with his conservative predecessor, Alain Juppe.
"Families betrayed", "Juppe thought it up, Jospin did it", "Children abandoned by Jospin", three of the banners said.
Jospin announced in parliament last Thursday that households earning more than 25,000 francs ($4,400) a month with two children would no longer receive the 667 franc ($117) monthly allowance.
The move was seen as a cautious first step towards making France's costly and largely indiscriminate welfare state more selective to focus more assistance on the lower-paid.

Officials said the measure would affect less than 10 percent of the 4.1 million families which receive the benefit, but ministers have since shown a certain disharmony in explaining or backpedalling on the decision.

Labour and Social Solidarity Minister Martine Aubry hastened to say that the figure announced by Jospin was "a basis for negotiation" and the threshold would be higher for families with three or more children.
But family associations, Christian groups and trade unions immediately expressed anger.

Communist parliamentary floor leader Alain Bocquet told reporters on Tuesday: "We have never been in favour of putting a ceiling on resources...The debate is now open, I hope that consultation will make possible a positive outcome."

Marc Blondel, leader of the non-partisan Force Ouvriere trade union, France's third biggest, said in a radio interview he was concerned that the move on family allowances might just be the thin end of the wedge prefiguring other restrictions.

"We in the trade unions are almost all hostile to capping benefits, given that the ceiling can vary. It could set a bad precedent for social security and health insurance," Blondel told Europe 1 radio.
